title: Floquet mobility edges and transport in a periodically driven generalized Aubry-André model
summary: We investigate the effect of a periodic electric field drive on the generalized Aubry-André model, also known as the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma (GPD) model, which is well known as a host of mobility edges. Our study of the Floquet spectrum of the driven GPD model uncovers the emergence of two distinct Floquet mobility edges, a delocalized--localized (DL) edge in the bounded regime, and a multifractal--localized (ML) edge in the unbounded regime. Using analytical results derived from Avila's global theory applied to the high frequency effective Hamiltonian, together with numerical diagnostics such as the fractal dimension and inverse participation ratio, we demonstrate that these mobility edges can be effectively controlled by the amplitude and frequency of the electric field drive. We also identify drive-induced localization at specific values of the driving parameters, corresponding to dynamical localization points in the absence of quasiperiodic potential. Furthermore, the dynamical study of the periodically driven GPD model demonstrates superdiffusive to almost ballistic transport in the bounded regime corresponding to the DL edges, whereas subdiffusive transport is observed in the unbounded regime associated with the ML edges. We also analyze deviations from the high-frequency effective description by explicitly examining the low-frequency driving regime, where significant and counterintuitive deviations in both spectral properties and transport behavior are observed. Our study highlights the interplay of a quasiperiodic potential and a periodically varying electric field drive as a powerful mechanism to engineer mobility edges and control transport in systems with rich spectral features.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how a periodic electric field drive affects the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma (GPD) model, revealing two distinct Floquet mobility edges (DL and ML) that can be controlled by driving parameters, with drive-induced localization and tunable transport from superdiffusive/ballistic to subdiffusive, while also examining deviations in the low-frequency regime.
AI.motivation: To understand and control mobility edges and transport in quasiperiodic systems with rich spectral features by leveraging the interplay between a quasiperiodic potential and a periodically varying electric field drive.
AI.method: Analytical Floquet analysis using Avila's global theory applied to the high-frequency effective Hamiltonian, combined with numerical diagnostics including fractal dimension and inverse participation ratio.
AI.result: Two distinct Floquet mobility edges emerge: a delocalized-localized (DL) edge in the bounded regime and a multifractal-localized (ML) edge in the unbounded regime. Drive-induced localization occurs at specific parameter values. Transport ranges from superdiffusive/ballistic (DL regime) to subdiffusive (ML regime). Low-frequency driving yields significant deviations from high-frequency predictions.
AI.conclusion: The periodic electric field drive serves as a powerful mechanism to engineer mobility edges and control transport in the GPD model, highlighting the rich interplay of quasiperiodic potentials and time-periodic driving.

title: A four-player potential game for barren-plateau-aware quantum ansatz design
summary: We cast the design of parameterized quantum circuits as a four-player potential game whose state is a circuit directed acyclic graph (DAG) and whose players encode trainability, non-stabilizerness, task performance, and hardware cost. Per-player restricted action sets factorize the move space into append, remove, retype, and rewire operations; a block-coordinate $\varepsilon$-Nash residual $δ_\text{Nash}$ certifies that no single player can improve unilaterally. A single weight sweep on MaxCut $K_4$ traces a Pareto frontier from a Clifford endpoint $(M_2/n,\langle H\rangle)=(0,4.00)$ to a non-Clifford endpoint $(0.48,3.30)$. On three four-qubit hardware topologies (heavy-hex, $2\times 2$ grid, Rydberg all-to-all), Nash search achieves the highest mean potential; on the $2\times 2$ grid Nash reaches the theoretical ceiling $Φ_\text{max}=4.10$ on two of five seeds while the simulated-annealing baseline does so on one; paired Wilcoxon tests over five seeds cannot reject the null on any single topology ($p\ge 0.22$). On LiH/STO-3G, seeding Nash from a 58-gate Givens-doubles ansatz produces a 48-operation, depth-25 circuit retaining $97.7\%$ of the correlation energy while simultaneously reducing gate count, increasing non-stabilizerness, and controlling trainability. The framework is complementary to energy-only searches such as ADAPT-VQE and k-UpCCGSD, which reach chemical accuracy with fewer operations but do not optimize the other three axes.

AI.tldr: Parameterized quantum circuit design is formulated as a four-player potential game optimizing trainability, non-stabilizerness, task performance, and hardware cost. Nash equilibrium search achieves Pareto-optimal circuits on MaxCut and chemistry benchmarks, outperforming baselines in multi-objective trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum circuit design methods (e.g., ADAPT-VQE) optimize solely for energy/task performance, ignoring other critical axes like trainability, non-stabilizerness (magic), and hardware cost, leading to circuits that may be untrainable or hardware-inefficient.
AI.method: Formulate circuit design as a four-player potential game on a circuit DAG. Players encode trainability (effective dimension), non-stabilizerness (M2/n), task performance (energy), and hardware cost (gate count/depth). Moves are append, remove, retype, rewire operations. Block-coordinate ε-Nash residual δ_Nash certifies no unilateral improvement.
AI.result: On MaxCut K4, Pareto frontier spans Clifford (M2/n=0) to non-Clifford (0.48). On 4-qubit hardware topologies, Nash search achieves highest mean potential; on 2×2 grid reaches theoretical ceiling Φ_max=4.10 (2/5 seeds) vs. SA baseline (1/5). On LiH/STO-3G, reduces 58-gate Givens ansatz to 48 ops, depth 25, retaining 97.7% correlation energy while improving other axes.
AI.conclusion: The game-theoretic framework provides complementary multi-objective optimization for quantum circuits, producing circuits that balance energy, trainability, magic, and hardware constraints—unlike energy-only methods that sacrifice other metrics for chemical accuracy.

title: Random entanglement percolation on realistic quantum networks
summary: We study random entanglement percolation in heterogeneous quantum networks, where the singlet-conversion probabilities (SCPs) of the edges are drawn from a probability distribution rather than being fixed. After briefly recalling random classical and random quantum entanglement percolation, we focus on polarization-dependent loss (PDL) as a physical source of random edge entanglement in photonic networks. In this setting, polarization imbalance induces a simple map from the PDL magnitude to the edge SCP. We illustrate this map for representative PDL models and discuss the resulting implications for entanglement percolation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies random entanglement percolation in heterogeneous quantum networks with variable singlet-conversion probabilities, focusing on polarization-dependent loss (PDL) in photonic networks as a physical source of random edge entanglement, mapping PDL magnitude to edge SCP and analyzing implications for percolation.
AI.motivation: To extend entanglement percolation theory to heterogeneous quantum networks where edge singlet-conversion probabilities are random variables rather than fixed constants, and to connect this theory to realistic physical imperfections like polarization-dependent loss in photonic systems.
AI.method: The authors review classical random percolation and random quantum entanglement percolation frameworks, then introduce polarization-dependent loss (PDL) as a physical mechanism generating random edge SCPs. They derive a mapping from PDL magnitude to edge SCP for representative PDL models.
AI.result: A simple mapping from PDL magnitude to edge SCP is established for photonic networks, with illustrations for representative PDL models showing how polarization imbalance translates into random edge entanglement properties.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal the implications of PDL-induced random edge SCPs for entanglement percolation thresholds and connectivity in heterogeneous quantum networks, providing a bridge between abstract percolation models and physical photonic implementations.

title: Expansion of time-convolutionless non-Markovian quantum master equations: A case study using the Fano-Anderson model
summary: We explore the performance of the time-convolutionless (TCL) projection operator technique using the Fano-Anderson model as a test case. Comparing the exact TCL master equation with an expansion in powers of the strength of the system-environment coupling, we analyze the transient dynamics as well as the steady-state behavior. For a Lorentzian spectral density we demonstrate that the dimensionless expansion parameter corresponds to the ratio of the environmental correlation time to the relaxation time of the system, and we derive the convergence radius for the TCL expansion, which is seen to depend on the ratio of detuning and width of the spectral density. We further study the quantum non-Markovianity of the model based on the evolution of the Bures distance between quantum states and how it is represented by the second and fourth order of the expansion. Our results highlight both the strengths and the limitations of the TCL formalism in capturing key features of open quantum systems and, in particular, the challenges of accurately describing strongly coupled systems and non-Markovian dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the time-convolutionless (TCL) projection operator technique using the Fano-Anderson model, analyzing its convergence radius, expansion validity in terms of system-environment coupling strength, and its ability (particularly at second and fourth order) to capture non-Markovian dynamics via Bures distance evolution.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate the strengths and limitations of the TCL projection operator technique for open quantum systems, particularly in strongly coupled and non-Markovian regimes.
AI.method: The Fano-Anderson model is used as a test case. The exact TCL master equation is compared against a perturbative expansion in powers of system-environment coupling strength. The dimensionless expansion parameter is identified as the ratio of environmental correlation time to system relaxation time. Convergence radius is derived analytically for a Lorentzian spectral density. Non-Markovianity is quantified via Bures distance evolution at second and fourth order of the expansion.
AI.result: For a Lorentzian spectral density, the convergence radius of the TCL expansion depends on the ratio of detuning to spectral width. The second and fourth order expansions capture non-Markovian features (via Bures distance) with varying fidelity, revealing limitations in strongly coupled regimes.
AI.conclusion: The TCL formalism has both strengths (systematic perturbative treatment) and limitations (challenges with strong coupling and accurately describing non-Markovian dynamics), providing guidance for its application in open quantum systems.

title: Entanglement and information scrambling in long-range measurement-only circuits
comment: 24 pages with appendices, 11 main text figures
summary:
Measurement-only circuits provide a minimal setting in which repeated local projections can either generate or suppress many-body entanglement, giving rise to measurement-induced phase transitions and dynamical regimes, that might have no unitary counterpart. Here we investigate entanglement and information transitions in one-dimensional measurement-only Clifford circuits with long-range two-qubit parity checks. By tuning both the measurement range and density per layer, we uncover a broad set of phases whose classification requires probes beyond entanglement entropy, such as mutual information, tripartite mutual information, purification from an ancilla, and Bell-cluster statistics. We map phase diagrams using large-scale Clifford simulations for two protocols: a random-basis design in which each measurement is randomly chosen from $\lbrace XX,YY,ZZ \rbrace$, and a single-basis design in which the basis is fixed within each layer but varies between layers, hence introducing more structure to the circuit.
  We map the trajectory-averaged entanglement entropy to a two-dimensional statistical mechanics model by extending a replica-based method to random-basis measurement-only circuits, and show that a continuous-time limit yields an effective long-range XX hamiltonian in the steady state. This connection links the observed volume-law to sub-volume-law entanglement transition to the boundary between a continuous symmetry broken phase and a critical XY phase. Strikingly, in structured (single-basis) circuits we find a phase in which volume-law and long-range entanglement coexists with rapid, size-independent purification of an ancilla qubit, and the absence of scrambling, highlighting measurement-only circuits as a promising route to efficiently preparing highly entangled and technologically useful quantum states.

AI.tldr: This paper studies measurement-only Clifford circuits with long-range parity checks in 1D, revealing rich phase diagrams beyond entanglement entropy using probes like mutual information and tripartite mutual information. The authors map entanglement transitions to a statistical mechanics model and find a surprising phase where volume-law entanglement coexists with fast purification and no scrambling.
AI.motivation: Measurement-only circuits provide a minimal setting to study how repeated local projections generate or suppress entanglement, potentially leading to phases with no unitary counterpart. The authors aim to classify the broad set of phases arising when measurement range and density are tuned.
AI.method: Large-scale Clifford simulations are used for two protocols: random-basis (measurements randomly chosen from {XX, YY, ZZ}) and single-basis (basis fixed per layer but varies between layers). Entanglement entropy is mapped to a 2D statistical mechanics model via a replica method; continuous-time limit yields an effective long-range XX Hamiltonian.
AI.result: A rich phase diagram is uncovered, including volume-law to sub-volume-law entanglement transitions linked to a symmetry breaking boundary. In single-basis circuits, a phase exhibits volume-law and long-range entanglement coexisting with rapid, size-independent ancilla purification and absence of scrambling.
AI.conclusion: Measurement-only circuits are a promising route for efficiently preparing highly entangled quantum states with technological utility, as demonstrated by the coexistence of volume-law entanglement and fast purification.

title: Tantalum Damascene Coplanar Waveguide Resonators Fabricated Using 300 mm Scale Processes
summary: Surface oxides contribute to losses in superconducting transmon devices resulting in degraded performance. We explore the use of the damascene process to replace the sidewall native oxide of a device with a metal/substrate interface. We simulate sidewall oxidation by burying an oxide layer during fabrication. We observe a modest improvement between the two types of devices, which is suggestive of a reduction in the surface participation ratio.

AI.tldr: Damascene process replaces sidewall native oxide with metal/substrate interface to reduce surface oxide losses in superconducting transmon devices, showing modest improvement suggestive of reduced surface participation ratio.
AI.motivation: Surface oxides cause performance degradation in superconducting transmon devices, motivating exploration of fabrication processes to mitigate these losses.
AI.method: The damascene process is used to replace sidewall native oxide with a metal/substrate interface; sidewall oxidation is simulated by burying an oxide layer during fabrication.
AI.result: A modest improvement between the two device types is observed, suggestive of a reduction in the surface participation ratio.
AI.conclusion: The damascene approach shows promise for reducing surface oxide-related losses in superconducting qubits, though improvements are modest.

title: Signature of paraparticles: a minimal Gedankenexperiment
summary: Paraparticles beyond bosons and fermions can be exchanged via either the braid group (anyons, existing up to $D=2$ space dimensions) or the permutation group; in the latter case the space dimensions are not limited. Besides being predicted, anyons have been experimentally detected. The situation differs for paraparticles exchanged via the permutation group ("permutation-group parastatistics").The first test to detect their theoretical signature was published in 2021 (for $Z_2\times Z_2$-graded parafermions; it was soon followed by a second paper proving the detectability of $Z_2\times Z_2$-graded parabosons). Later on, two further papers proved theoretical signatures of permutation-group parastatistics. These works demonstrate that, in certain situations, a long-held belief on the "conventionality of parastatistics" argument can be evaded: some measurements of permutation-group paraparticles cannot be recovered from ordinary bosons/fermions. The main question now is how to experimentally detect or engineer in the laboratory such paraparticles. For this aim a minimal setup for the theoretical test is here provided: a Gedankenexperiment (a simplified version of the two tests published in 2021) which, essentially, is a flow chart of logical operations. The key point is to present, to experimentalists, the necessary steps to be simulated/realized in the laboratory (possibly, by manipulating qudits). In this minimal setup, the detection/engineering of paraparticles is mapped into a chirality test. The mathematical setting is based on $Z_2\times Z_2$-graded color Lie (super)algebras and derived mathematical structures.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a minimal experimental setup (Gedankenexperiment) for detecting permutation-group paraparticles, mapping the problem to a chirality test using Z₂×Z₂-graded color Lie superalgebras, building on theoretical signatures from 2021 that evade the conventionality of parastatistics argument.
AI.motivation: The main question is how to experimentally detect or engineer permutation-group paraparticles in the laboratory, given that theoretical signatures have been proven but no experimental realization exists yet.
AI.method: A Gedankenexperiment is designed as a minimal setup: a flow chart of logical operations that maps the detection/engineering of paraparticles into a chirality test, based on Z₂×Z₂-graded color Lie superalgebras.
AI.result: The theoretical detection problem is reduced to a chirality test, providing experimentalists with necessary steps to simulate or realize the detection using qudit manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Permutation-group paraparticles can be experimentally detected via a chirality test in a minimal logical setup, moving beyond the long-held belief in the conventionality of parastatistics.

title: Constant Factor Analysis of Optimal Quantum Linear Solvers in Practice
summary: Optimal quantum linear equation solvers provide complexity $O(κ\log(1/ε))$, where $κ$ is the condition number and $ε$ is the allowable error. The optimal solver using a discrete adiabatic approach [PRX Quantum \textbf{3}, 040303 (2022)] has large analytically proven constant factors for the upper bound on the complexity. The constant factors were later found to be about 1,200 times smaller in numerical testing [Quantum \textbf{9}, 1887 (2025)]. This meant it is about an order of magnitude more efficient than using a randomised approach from [PRX Quantum \textbf{6}, 040373 (2025)], which has far smaller analytically proven constant factors. Recently, a ``Shortcut'' method has been found to provide an optimal solver which also has small proven constant factors. In the present work, we conduct a comprehensive numerical analysis comparing this method with the adiabatic solver for two families of random linear systems. We find that, in the case where the solution norm is \emph{unknown}, the adiabatic solver provides slightly better performance. If the solution norm is \emph{known}, then the shortcut method provides significantly better performance for non-Hermitian matrices.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically compares two optimal quantum linear equation solvers: the adiabatic approach and the "Shortcut" method, finding that the adiabatic solver performs slightly better when solution norm is unknown, while the Shortcut method provides significantly better performance for non-Hermitian matrices when solution norm is known.
AI.motivation: To conduct a comprehensive numerical analysis comparing the adiabatic quantum linear solver (which has large proven constant factors but empirically performs well) with the newly proposed "Shortcut" method (which has small proven constant factors), to determine which approach is more efficient in practice for random linear systems.
AI.method: Comprehensive numerical analysis comparing the adiabatic solver and the Shortcut method on two families of random linear systems, testing scenarios where solution norm is unknown versus known.
AI.result: When solution norm is unknown, the adiabatic solver provides slightly better performance. When solution norm is known, the Shortcut method provides significantly better performance for non-Hermitian matrices.
AI.conclusion: The choice of optimal quantum linear equation solver depends on prior knowledge: the adiabatic solver is preferable when solution norm is unknown, while the Shortcut method is significantly better for non-Hermitian matrices when solution norm is known.

title: Qubit-Scalable CVRP via Lagrangian Knapsack Decomposition and Noise-Aware Quantum Execution
summary: Hybrid quantum optimization for vehicle routing faces a practical bottleneck: direct QUBO encodings of CVRP quickly exceed near-term qubit and gate budgets, while quantum evaluations are expensive, noise-limited, and sensitive to backend and circuit configuration. We address this gap with an end-to-end decomposition pipeline that converts CVRP into bounded-width quantum subproblems and treats quantum execution as a decision problem within the optimization loop. Starting from a Fisher--Jaikumar assignment linearization, we apply Lagrangian relaxation to dualize customer-assignment couplers, yielding independent per-vehicle knapsack subproblems that admit QUBO/Ising evaluation. To replace brittle subgradient tuning, we learn a multiplier-update controller using expert-guided pretraining followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, with rewards based on execution-realized progress and route reconstruction. We also introduce a constrained contextual bandit as a hardware-aware execution layer that selects backend and circuit configuration with feasibility screening, enabling adaptation across heterogeneous noisy resources and parallel multi-QPU scheduling. Computational results on multiple CVRPLIB families show that the decomposition yields stable bounded-width subproblems across instance sizes, learned multiplier updates improve end-to-end routing quality relative to classical subgradient control under matched budgets, and hardware-mode configuration reduces median optimality gaps relative to static execution choices in our test set. We do not claim quantum advantage. Instead, the contribution is a practical end-to-end framework for scaling hybrid quantum CVRP optimization through OR decomposition, learning-augmented dual control, and adaptive hardware-aware execution.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum optimization pipeline for CVRP that combines Fisher-Jaikumar decomposition, Lagrangian relaxation, learned multiplier updates (expert pretraining + RL fine-tuning), and a contextual bandit for hardware-aware backend/circuit selection, producing stable bounded-width QUBO subproblems.
AI.motivation: Direct QUBO encodings of CVRP exceed near-term qubit/gate budgets, and quantum evaluations are expensive, noise-limited, and sensitive to backend and circuit configuration.
AI.method: (1) Fisher-Jaikumar assignment linearization → Lagrangian relaxation to decouple customer-assignment couplers → independent per-vehicle knapsack QUBO subproblems. (2) Learned multiplier-update controller via expert-guided pretraining + RL fine-tuning with execution-realized progress rewards. (3) Constrained contextual bandit for hardware-aware execution layer (backend + circuit config selection with feasibility screening, parallel multi-QPU scheduling).
AI.result: Stable bounded-width subproblems across CVRPLIB instances; learned multiplier updates improve routing quality over classical subgradient control under matched budgets; hardware-mode configuration reduces median optimality gaps vs. static execution choices.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a practical end-to-end framework for scaling hybrid quantum CVRP through OR decomposition, learning-augmented dual control, and adaptive hardware-aware execution — no quantum advantage is claimed.

title: On the Interplay Between Noise, Bell Violation, and Cascade Error Correction in Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution
comment: 6 pages. This paper is submitted to Green Technology and Sustainable Development (GTSD2026)
summary: Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD) provides information-theoretic security by relying solely on the violation of Bell inequalities, eliminating the need to trust the quantum devices. However, practical implementations of DIQKD are highly sensitive to noise. Efficient error correction during the classical post-processing stage is important for improving the fidelity. This work investigates the impact of noise on the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) value and evaluates the effectiveness of Cascade error correction. The protocol is applied iteratively to correct errors via parity checking and binary search procedures. Simulation results show that noise significantly degrades the CHSH value, reducing the strength of nonlocal correlations required for secure DIQKD. Nevertheless, Cascade reduces the error ratio, and most corrections occur within the first several rounds. These findings highlight the importance of classical error correction in improving DIQKD systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how noise degrades the CHSH value in DIQKD and evaluates Cascade error correction for improving key fidelity, finding that Cascade effectively reduces error ratios with most corrections occurring in early rounds.
AI.motivation: DIQKD provides information-theoretic security without trusting quantum devices, but practical implementations are highly sensitive to noise, motivating the need for efficient error correction in classical post-processing.
AI.method: The authors analyze noise impact on CHSH values and apply Cascade error correction iteratively via parity checking and binary search procedures.
AI.result: Noise significantly degrades the CHSH value, reducing nonlocal correlations. Cascade successfully reduces the error ratio, with most corrections occurring in the first several rounds.
AI.conclusion: Classical error correction, particularly Cascade, is important for improving the fidelity and practical viability of DIQKD systems under noisy conditions.

title: Certification of genuine non-Gaussian entanglement
summary: Entanglement is a key resource for many quantum applications. Understanding fundamental properties of entangled states is an important step towards their practical exploitation. We characterize entanglement in the context of Gaussian and non-Gaussian processes and identify entangled states that cannot be produced by any Gaussian evolution acting on separable states. This distinction exposes intrinsic limitations of Gaussian operations and highlights the role of non-Gaussian operations as an important resource. We apply this framework to develop a certification method that connects entanglement theory with quantum non-Gaussianity - an advanced quantum feature that is essential for several quantum applications. Our approach tailors the certification to experimentally relevant states that can be produced in current quantum optics experiments. We demonstrate this certification for recognizing the genuine non-Gaussian entanglement of various entangled Fock states and hybrid entangled states.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes entanglement in Gaussian vs. non-Gaussian processes, identifying entangled states that cannot be produced by Gaussian evolution alone, and develops a certification method linking entanglement theory with quantum non-Gaussianity for experimentally relevant states.
AI.motivation: To understand fundamental properties of entangled states and expose the intrinsic limitations of Gaussian operations, thereby highlighting non-Gaussian operations as a crucial resource for quantum applications.
AI.method: The framework connects entanglement theory with quantum non-Gaussianity, tailoring certification to experimentally relevant states producible in current quantum optics experiments. The method is demonstrated on entangled Fock states and hybrid entangled states.
AI.result: Identification of entangled states that cannot be produced by any Gaussian evolution from separable states, and successful certification of genuine non-Gaussian entanglement for various entangled Fock states and hybrid entangled states.
AI.conclusion: Non-Gaussian operations are an essential resource for producing certain entangled states, and the proposed certification method effectively recognizes genuine non-Gaussian entanglement in experimentally accessible states.

title: An efficient framework for quantum dynamics driven by nonclassical light
summary: Understanding quantum system dynamics driven by nonclassical light pulses is challenging, particularly for general light states with large photon numbers. Here we introduce an efficient framework that makes this task tractable. By introducing a pulse-shaped P-representation, the exact quantum evolution is decomposed into a mixture of many independent quasi-classical branches, each governed by a standard master equation with a classical pulse which can be solved efficiently. As an illustration, for a two-level system interacting with an exponential pulse, we first find out the exact analytical solutions to the Bloch equations in each quasi-classical branch, and then by taking proper P-function average over all branches, the full system dynamics driven by nonclassical light pulses is analytically obtained. For the one-photon and two-photon cases, our method well reproduces the previous exact results either analytically or numerically. Crucially, our approach scales efficiently to more complex light states (Fock, thermal, squeezed vacuum states) with large photon numbers ($N\sim 100$). We further provide a clear physical interpretation how the system dynamics is influenced through the high-order optical coherence of the nonclassical pulses. This work provides a unified and computationally efficient route and a useful starting point to explore more complex quantum dynamics driven by nonclassical light in quantum optics and quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a pulse-shaped P-representation framework that decomposes quantum system dynamics driven by nonclassical light pulses into independent quasi-classical branches, enabling efficient analytical and numerical solutions for complex light states with large photon numbers (up to N~100).
AI.motivation: Understanding quantum system dynamics driven by nonclassical light pulses is challenging, particularly for general light states with large photon numbers.
AI.method: A pulse-shaped P-representation is introduced to decompose exact quantum evolution into a mixture of independent quasi-classical branches, each governed by a standard master equation with a classical pulse. Analytical solutions to Bloch equations are derived for each branch, and P-function averaging over branches yields full system dynamics.
AI.result: For one-photon and two-photon cases, the method reproduces previous exact results. The approach scales efficiently to more complex light states (Fock, thermal, squeezed vacuum states) with large photon numbers (N~100).
AI.conclusion: This work provides a unified, computationally efficient route and a useful starting point to explore complex quantum dynamics driven by nonclassical light in quantum optics and quantum information processing.

title: Entanglement Enhanced Sensing with Qubits affected by non-Markovian Dephasing
summary: Entanglement has been proposed as a means to improve the sensitivity of sensing weak signals. While the degree of this quantum advantage is well understood in noiseless settings, the situation is more complex under realistic conditions, where the system is subject to decoherence. In this case, the enhancement depends on the specific noise characteristics. Previous treatments of colored noise typically assume that the noise is uncorrelated between successive experiments. Here, we consider the scenario in which the noise exhibits correlations across multiple shots. We derive a simple fundamental limit to the sensitivity based on the fact that the sensitivity cannot be better than the signal-to-noise ratio seen by the probe. Focusing on Ramsey spectroscopy with probes affected by pure classical dephasing, we show that, for suitable spatial and temporal noise correlations, entangled probes achieve a better scaling of the sensitivity with the number of probes than separable states. This demonstrates that entanglement can provide a substantial improvement for Ramsey spectroscopy subject to correlated noise.

AI.tldr: Entanglement improves sensing sensitivity under correlated noise, with entangled probes achieving better scaling than separable states in Ramsey spectroscopy with classical dephasing.
AI.motivation: To understand how entanglement can enhance sensing sensitivity under realistic noisy conditions, specifically when noise exhibits correlations across multiple experimental shots, going beyond previous treatments that assumed uncorrelated noise.
AI.method: The authors derive a fundamental sensitivity limit based on the signal-to-noise ratio seen by the probe. They analyze Ramsey spectroscopy with probes affected by pure classical dephasing, studying both spatial and temporal noise correlations for entangled versus separable states.
AI.result: For suitable spatial and temporal noise correlations, entangled probes achieve a better scaling of sensitivity with the number of probes compared to separable states.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement can provide substantial improvement for Ramsey spectroscopy under correlated noise conditions, contrary to simpler noiseless or uncorrelated-noise scenarios.

title: No-Go Theorem for Quantum Heat Engines Powered Purely by Quantum Measurements in the Steady Regime
summary: We study the thermodynamics of a quantum measurement-powered engine that converts energy injected by measurement backaction into work. We consider an engine with a finite-dimensional working substance, driven purely by quantum measurements, i.e., by bare quantum measurements, without feedback control or thermal contact in the thermodynamic cycle. On the basis of a Poincaré-like recurrence theorem for general quantum channels, we prove a no-go result for work extraction from such an engine in the steady regime. In the steady regime, quantum measurements become nondisturbing and do not inject energy into the working substance. Consequently, no work can be extracted. This result reveals the necessity of an entropy-decreasing process, such as feedback control or thermal contact, for work extraction in steady-cycle measurement-powered engines.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a no-go theorem showing that a quantum measurement-powered engine without feedback control or thermal contact cannot extract work in the steady regime, as measurements become nondisturbing and cease to inject energy.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental thermodynamic limits of engines powered solely by quantum measurement backaction, and to determine whether work extraction is possible without additional entropy-decreasing processes like feedback or thermal contact.
AI.method: The authors analyze a quantum measurement-powered engine with a finite-dimensional working substance, driven by bare quantum measurements. They employ a Poincaré-like recurrence theorem for general quantum channels to prove their no-go result.
AI.result: In the steady regime, quantum measurements become nondisturbing and do not inject energy into the working substance, making work extraction impossible. No work can be extracted from such an engine without feedback control or thermal contact.
AI.conclusion: An entropy-decreasing process (e.g., feedback control or thermal contact) is necessary for work extraction in steady-cycle measurement-powered engines, establishing a fundamental limitation for purely measurement-driven thermodynamic cycles.

title: Two flavor neutrino oscillations in presence of non-Hermitian dynamics
summary: We develop a consistent mathematical framework for studying two flavor neutrino oscillations in presence of non-Hermitian dynamics. We consider two approaches : (a) bi-orthonormal inner product defined by a positive-definite metric operator $\mathcal{G}$ and (b) the density matrix prescription by Brody and Graefe [Phys. Rev. Lett. 109, 230405 (2012)]. For the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric case, we show that the $\mathcal{G}$ metric approach does not work well (probabilities are not conserved) both in $\mathcal{PT}$-unbroken as well as $\mathcal{PT}$-broken regime. Hence, we adopt the density matrix prescription by Brody and Graefe which is a positive semi-definite map. In the density matrix prescription, we note that probability in the steady state limit is not necessarily $1/2$ thereby indicating non-Markovian behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a mathematical framework for two-flavor neutrino oscillations with non-Hermitian dynamics, comparing a metric-operator approach and a density-matrix approach. The metric approach fails for PT-symmetric cases, while the density matrix prescription yields non-Markovian steady-state probabilities not equal to 1/2.
AI.motivation: To establish a consistent mathematical framework for two-flavor neutrino oscillations under non-Hermitian (specifically PT-symmetric) dynamics, as standard Hermitian quantum mechanics may not adequately describe certain neutrino phenomena.
AI.method: Two approaches are compared: (a) a bi-orthonormal inner product using a positive-definite metric operator G, and (b) the Brody-Graefe density matrix prescription (a positive semi-definite map).
AI.result: The G-metric approach fails in both PT-unbroken and PT-broken regimes (probabilities are not conserved). The density matrix prescription works and shows steady-state probabilities are not necessarily 1/2.
AI.conclusion: The Brody-Graefe density matrix prescription is the appropriate framework for non-Hermitian neutrino oscillations, revealing non-Markovian behavior where steady-state probabilities deviate from 1/2.

title: Quantum analog-encoding for correlated Gaussian vectors and their exponentiation with application to rough volatility
summary: Quantum computing may speed up numerical problems involving large matrices that are demanding for classical computers, and active research on this possibility is ongoing. In this work, we propose quantum algorithms for the exact simulation of a normalised correlated Gaussian random vector $|x\rangle=\vec{x}/\lVert\vec{x}\rVert$, $\vec{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Σ)$, and its exponentiation $|e^{\vec{x}} \rangle= e^{\vec{x}}/\lVert e^{\vec{x}}\rVert$. When an $O(\mathrm{polylog} N)$-gate-depth quantum data loader for the covariance matrix $Σ\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ is available, preparing $|x\rangle$ and $|e^{\vec{x}}\rangle$ require $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{\lVertΣ\rVert_F}{λ_{\max}}κ^{1.5}\right)$ and $\widetilde{O}\left(\lVert\vec{x}\rVert\frac{\lVertΣ\rVert_F}{λ_{\max}}κ^{1.5}\right)$ elementary gate depth respectively, where $\lVertΣ\rVert_F$, $λ_{\max}$, $κ$ denote the Frobenius norm, maximal eigenvalue, and condition number of $Σ$. Motivated by financial applications, we provide an end-to-end resource analysis when $\vec{x}$ represents a sample path of a Riemann-Liouville or standard fractional Brownian motion, or of a stationary fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. As a concrete example, we construct the quantum state encoding the rough Bergomi variance process and analyse the extraction of the integrated variance via quantum amplitude estimation. Under specific conditions, the dependence of $\lVertΣ\rVert_F/λ_{\max}$ and $κ$ on $N$ is small, and subcubic complexity in $N$ is achieved, indicating a quantum advantage over classical Cholesky-based sampling methods. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first quantum algorithmic framework for the amplitude encoding of exponentiated Gaussian processes, providing foundational primitives for quantum-enhanced financial modelling.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes quantum algorithms for preparing normalized correlated Gaussian random vectors and their exponentiated versions, achieving subcubic complexity in N when efficient quantum data loaders are available, with applications to financial modeling (e.g., rough Bergomi variance process).
AI.motivation: Quantum computing may accelerate numerical problems involving large matrices that are computationally demanding for classical computers. This work is motivated by financial applications requiring efficient simulation of Gaussian random vectors and their exponentials, e.g., for volatility modeling in option pricing.
AI.method: The authors propose quantum algorithms that, given an O(polylog N)-gate-depth quantum data loader for covariance matrix Σ, prepare |x⟩ (normalized Gaussian vector) and |e^x⟩ (its exponentiation) with gate depths scaling as Õ(‖Σ‖_F/λ_max * κ^{1.5}) and Õ(‖x‖ * ‖Σ‖_F/λ_max * κ^{1.5}) respectively. They apply this to Riemann-Liouville/standard fractional Brownian motion and stationary fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, constructing the rough Bergomi variance process and extracting integrated variance via quantum amplitude estimation.
AI.result: Under specific conditions, the dependence of ‖Σ‖_F/λ_max and κ on N is small, leading to subcubic complexity in N, indicating a quantum advantage over classical Cholesky-based sampling. This is the first quantum algorithmic framework for amplitude encoding of exponentiated Gaussian processes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum algorithms provide foundational primitives for quantum-enhanced financial modelling, enabling efficient simulation of Gaussian processes and their exponentials that are central to many quantitative finance applications.

title: Boundary-Aware Stabilizer Scheduling for Distributed Quantum Error Correction
summary:
Future quantum architectures are expected to be modular, with quantum processors connecting multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) via photonic interconnects. In topological quantum error correction, such as color codes, this creates seam boundaries where parity checks require remote CNOT operations using heralded Bell pairs. These non-local checks are slower and noisier than bulk local checks because entanglement generation is probabilistic, causing data qubits to accumulate idle noise while waiting for remote operations. A natural way to reduce this overhead is to skip some seam measurements; however, doing so makes seam syndrome information stale and can degrade decoding. The central scheduling problem is therefore to determine how frequently seam checks should be measured so as to balance remote-operation and waiting noise against syndrome staleness.
  To address this trade-off, we develop a scheduling module that integrates directly into standard syndrome-extraction circuits. We consider two policies: Skip-Seam-$τ$ (SS-$τ$), which measures all bulk checks every round while measuring seam checks once every $τ$ rounds and copying the most recent syndrome in skipped rounds, and Adaptive Skip-$τ$ (AST), which selects $τ$ as a function of code distance and entanglement generation rate (EGR). We evaluate these policies on triangular color codes under circuit-level noise in Stim, including idling errors induced by Bell-pair generation delays. Our simulations show that SS-tau and AST reduce remote-operation overhead and can lower the logical error rate (LER) relative to the Measure-All (MA) baseline. For physical error rate $p = 10^{-3}$, we identify an EGR regime in which both SS-$τ$ and AST exhibit behavior consistent with fault-tolerant scaling, with LER decreasing as code distance increases. Across these regimes, SS-$τ$ and AST outperform MA.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the scheduling problem in modular quantum architectures with topological color codes, where seam boundaries require slower, noisier remote CNOT operations. Two scheduling policies (SS-$τ$ and AST) that skip some seam measurements are proposed to balance remote-operation/waiting noise against syndrome staleness. Simulations show these policies reduce remote-operation overhead and lower logical error rates compared to the Measure-All baseline.
AI.motivation: Future quantum architectures will be modular with multiple QPUs connected via photonic interconnects. In topological quantum error correction (color codes), seam boundaries require remote CNOT operations using heralded Bell pairs, which are slower and noisier than bulk local checks due to probabilistic entanglement generation. This causes data qubits to accumulate idle noise while waiting, creating a need to balance measurement frequency against noise.
AI.method: Develops a scheduling module integrated into standard syndrome-extraction circuits. Proposes two policies: (1) Skip-Seam-$τ$ (SS-$τ$), which measures all bulk checks every round but seam checks once every $τ$ round with syndrome copying in skipped rounds; (2) Adaptive Skip-$τ$ (AST), which selects $τ$ based on code distance and entanglement generation rate (EGR). Evaluated on triangular color codes under circuit-level noise in Stim including idling errors from Bell-pair generation delays.
AI.result: SS-$τ$ and AST reduce remote-operation overhead and lower logical error rate (LER) relative to Measure-All baseline. For physical error rate $p=10^{-3}$, both policies exhibit fault-tolerant scaling behavior (LER decreases with code distance) in certain EGR regimes, outperforming the MA baseline.
AI.conclusion: Skipping seam measurements strategically (SS-$τ$ and AST) is an effective approach to balance the trade-off between remote-operation/waiting noise and syndrome staleness in modular quantum architectures, yielding lower logical error rates than always measuring all checks.

title: Double Slit Experiment in the Heisenberg Picture of Quantum Mechanics
summary: We present the standard double slit experiment with non-relativistic particles in the Heisenberg Picture of quantum mechanics. Our motivation is threefold. First and foremost, and contrary to some claims in the literature, we show that there is no need to talk about non-locality when explaining the interference fringes. Secondly, we emphasise the fact that even in the non-relativistic regime, and in order to preserve locality, we should define the position and momentum observables of a particle as functions of both space and time (and not just time). Thirdly, our presentation compares the projective measurements in the Heisenberg picture with the "Church of the Larger Hilbert Space", the latter of which is seldom discussed in the Heisenberg picture of quantum mechanics.

AI.tldr: The paper reexamines the double slit experiment in the Heisenberg Picture, arguing that interference fringes can be explained without invoking non-locality, by defining observables as functions of both space and time, and comparing projective measurements with the Church of the Larger Hilbert Space.
AI.motivation: Threefold: (1) to show that interference fringes do not require non-locality explanations, contrary to claims in the literature; (2) to argue that even in non-relativistic quantum mechanics, preserving locality requires position and momentum observables to be functions of both space and time; (3) to compare projective measurements in the Heisenberg picture with the Church of the Larger Hilbert Space approach.
AI.method: The paper uses the Heisenberg Picture formulation of quantum mechanics to analyze the standard double slit experiment with non-relativistic particles.
AI.result: Interference fringes can be explained locally in the Heisenberg Picture without invoking non-locality. Position and momentum observables must be defined as functions of both space and time to maintain locality.
AI.conclusion: The Heisenberg Picture provides a local account of the double slit experiment, and the comparison with the Church of the Larger Hilbert Space offers additional insights into measurement theory.

title: Programming long-range interactions in analog quantum simulators
summary: Long-range interactions are the source of many equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium quantum many-body phenomena. Analog simulators based on ionic, atomic, superconducting, and molecular systems provide a natural platform to obtain these interactions using vibration- and photon-mediated processes. Recent experimental advances, such as their integration in multi-mode cavities and waveguides, or the use of Raman-assisted transitions, enable dynamical control over both the strength and the spatial range of these interactions, thereby rendering them programmable. Here, we develop a hybrid classical-quantum toolbox that exploits this tunability to enhance many-body state preparation in analog simulators beyond fixed-connectivity architectures. Our approach is based on classical pre-compilation in homogeneous small systems, whose optimized parameters are extrapolated iteratively to larger system sizes, and then refined on the quantum hardware using noise-aware hybrid re-optimization and error-mitigation techniques. We benchmark this strategy across several fermionic, spin-1/2, and spin-1 models, demonstrating orders-of-magnitude improvements in fidelity and energy estimation for system sizes ranging from 100 to 1000 particles. Finally, we show that the combination of such high-fidelity programmable state preparation techniques with tunable-range out-of-equilibrium dynamics enables controlled studies of many-body thermalization in regimes accessible to current experimental platforms. Our results establish programmable long-range interactions as a powerful resource for next-generation analog quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a hybrid classical-quantum toolbox that leverages programmable long-range interactions to enhance many-body state preparation in analog quantum simulators, achieving orders-of-magnitude improvements in fidelity and energy estimation for systems of 100-1000 particles across fermionic, spin-1/2, and spin-1 models.
AI.motivation: Long-range interactions are a key source of many-body phenomena, and recent experimental advances now allow dynamical control over their strength and spatial range. The authors aim to exploit this tunability to overcome limitations of fixed-connectivity architectures in analog simulators for many-body state preparation.
AI.method: A hybrid classical-quantum approach: classical pre-compilation in small homogeneous systems, iterative extrapolation of optimized parameters to larger sizes, then refinement on quantum hardware using noise-aware hybrid re-optimization and error-mitigation techniques.
AI.result: Orders-of-magnitude improvements in fidelity and energy estimation for system sizes from 100 to 1000 particles across fermionic, spin-1/2, and spin-1 models. Combined with tunable-range out-of-equilibrium dynamics, the approach enables controlled studies of many-body thermalization in currently accessible experimental platforms.
AI.conclusion: Programmable long-range interactions are established as a powerful resource for next-generation analog quantum simulators, enabling high-fidelity state preparation and controlled thermalization studies beyond what fixed-connectivity architectures can achieve.

title: Quantum limits on squeezing
summary: In our work, we show how, for a network of bosonic modes, canonical commutation relations constrain the coefficients relating input and internal modes. Based on these constraints, we derive a lower bound on the total steady-state squeezing achievable in reservoir-engineered (dissipative) squeezing schemes, quantified by the sum of mode-optimal quadrature variances normalized to its corresponding input variance. The bound follows solely from canonical commutation relations and stability, and is saturated in the strong-coupling limit at 1. Furthermore, we show that adding independent parametric driving terms for each mode changes the quantum noise-gain balance and yields a distinct optimum bound, approaching 1/2. In addition, we show how these constraints allow us to reformulate the Duan inseparability criterion for a three-mode bosonic system in terms of a single parameter-dependent figure of merit. Our results apply directly to current electromechanical and nanomechanical experiments and indicate that the two-mode bounds can be experimentally approached even at room temperature.

AI.tldr: The paper derives fundamental bounds on squeezing in reservoir-engineered bosonic networks from canonical commutation relations, showing a bound of 1 in the strong-coupling limit and 1/2 with parametric driving, and reformulates the Duan inseparability criterion for three-mode systems.
AI.motivation: To establish fundamental limits on squeezing achievable in dissipative bosonic networks based solely on canonical commutation relations and stability constraints, and to understand how parametric driving alters these bounds.
AI.method: The authors use canonical commutation relations to derive constraints on input-output mode coefficients, from which they compute lower bounds on steady-state squeezing via quadrature variance sums. They also reformulate the Duan inseparability criterion for three-mode systems using these constraints.
AI.result: The bound on total steady-state squeezing is saturated at 1 in the strong-coupling limit without parametric driving, and approaches 1/2 with independent parametric driving. The two-mode bounds are experimentally approachable even at room temperature in electromechanical and nanomechanical systems.
AI.conclusion: Canonical commutation relations impose fundamental constraints on dissipative squeezing that can be saturated experimentally, with parametric driving offering a distinct advantage (bound of 1/2 vs. 1). The framework also extends to multi-mode entanglement criteria.

title: Decohered color code and emerging mixed toric code by anyon proliferation: Topological entanglement negativity perspective
summary: We study how the color code under decoherence gives rise to an intrinsic mixed-state topological order (imTO), which has no counterpart in pure ground states of local gapped Hamiltonians. For decoherence induced by XX-type operators on red links of the honeycomb lattice, we show that the resulting mixed state inherits half of the topological properties of the color code, including anyon content, logical operators, and topological entanglement structure. Using a gauging procedure for mixed stabilizer states, we identify the emergent phase as closely related to a single toric code. We characterize this phase by topological entanglement negativity (TEN) and perform efficient stabilizer-formalism simulations. While the pure color code has ${\rm TEN} = 2 \ln 2$, the maximally decohered state has ${\rm TEN} = \ln 2$, indicating emergence of a single toric code. By tuning the decoherence strength, we find a smooth crossover in TEN accompanied by a pronounced, nearly system-size-independent peak in its variance. We further show that the negativity exhibits characteristic scaling only for subsystem partitions commensurate with the triangular lattice of the emergent toric code. Our results demonstrate that negativity-based quantities provide powerful probes of mixed-state topological order generated by decoherence.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the color code under decoherence (XX-type operators on red links of the honeycomb lattice) transitions into an intrinsic mixed-state topological order (imTO) that resembles a single toric code, characterized by topological entanglement negativity (TEN) changing from 2 ln 2 (pure color code) to ln 2 (maximally decohered state), with a crossover and size-independent variance peak.
AI.motivation: To understand how mixed-state topological orders emerge from decoherence of topologically ordered systems (specifically the color code), and to identify whether such mixed states can host intrinsic topological order that has no pure-state counterpart.
AI.method: The authors analyze decoherence via XX-type operators on red links of the honeycomb lattice, employ a gauging procedure for mixed stabilizer states, perform efficient stabilizer-formalism simulations, and use topological entanglement negativity (TEN) as the diagnostic quantity.
AI.result: The mixed state inherits half the topological properties of the color code (anyon content, logical operators, topological entanglement structure). TEN transitions from 2 ln 2 (pure) to ln 2 (maximally decohered), indicating a single emergent toric code. A smooth crossover with a pronounced, nearly system-size-independent variance peak appears. Negativity shows characteristic scaling only for subsystem partitions commensurate with the emergent toric code's triangular lattice.
AI.conclusion: Negativity-based quantities are powerful probes of mixed-state topological order generated by decoherence, and the color code under decoherence yields an intrinsic mixed-state topological order equivalent to a single toric code.

title: On truncations of hierarchical equations of motion for finite-dimensional systems
summary: We study truncations of hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) for finite-dimensional open quantum systems. We prove that for finite-dimensional approximations constructed with a Schur-complement type of terminator, the spectrum converges to that of the full HEOM as the truncation depth increases. We also prove that this approximation is free of spectral pollution: sufficiently deep truncations do not produce spurious unstable modes, provided the exact HEOM is stable. We illustrate the results for the spin-boson model.

AI.tldr: The paper studies truncations of hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) for finite-dimensional open quantum systems, proving spectral convergence and absence of spectral pollution when using Schur-complement-type terminators, with illustration on the spin-boson model.
AI.motivation: To rigorously establish the spectral properties of truncated HEOM approximations, specifically convergence and the absence of spurious unstable modes (spectral pollution), which are critical for reliable numerical simulations of open quantum systems.
AI.method: The authors analyze finite-dimensional approximations of HEOM using a Schur-complement type of terminator. They prove spectral convergence as truncation depth increases and show that sufficiently deep truncations are free of spectral pollution if the exact HEOM is stable. Numerical illustration is provided for the spin-boson model.
AI.result: The spectrum of the truncated HEOM converges to that of the full HEOM as truncation depth increases. No spurious unstable modes appear in sufficiently deep truncations when the exact system is stable.
AI.conclusion: Schur-complement-type terminators provide a reliable truncation scheme for HEOM, ensuring both spectral convergence and absence of spectral pollution, making them suitable for numerical simulations of open quantum dynamics.

title: Analytical and Compressed Simulation of Noisy Stabilizer Circuits
summary: We develop analytical and algorithmic techniques that enable efficient simulation of a broad class of noisy stabilizer circuits. We derive closed-form expressions of expectation values for tensor product of Paulis in circuits with non-deterministic Pauli measurements, yielding an efficient strong simulation method that avoids explicit density matrix construction and enables direct noise parameter sweeps. We introduce a circuit compression framework that reduces the per-sample cost of weak simulation in general noisy stabilizer circuits, including deterministic measurements, by separating parameter-independent preprocessing from sampling. Finally, we extend the analytical framework beyond its standard domain to include a small number of deterministic measurements, general rotations, and non-diagonal noise channels. Our results provide a unified framework for both strong and weak simulation of noisy stabilizer circuits and corresponds to an extension of the noisy stabilizer formalism introduced in \cite{PhysRevA.107.032424}. They offer applications ranging from calculation of the expectation values of entanglement witnesses, determination of reduced states, to energy evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops analytical and algorithmic techniques for efficient simulation of noisy stabilizer circuits, providing closed-form expectation values for Pauli products, a circuit compression framework for weak simulation, and extensions beyond standard domains, offering a unified framework for both strong and weak simulation.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient simulation of noisy stabilizer circuits, which are important for near-term quantum computing but computationally expensive under noise, and to avoid explicit density matrix construction.
AI.method: Closed-form expressions for expectation values of tensor product Paulis in circuits with non-deterministic Pauli measurements; circuit compression framework separating parameter-independent preprocessing from sampling; extension to deterministic measurements, general rotations, and non-diagonal noise channels.
AI.result: Efficient strong simulation avoiding explicit density matrices, enabling direct noise parameter sweeps; reduced per-sample cost for weak simulation via circuit compression; extended applicability beyond standard noisy stabilizer formalism.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified framework for strong and weak simulation of noisy stabilizer circuits, with applications including expectation values of entanglement witnesses, reduced state determination, and energy evaluation.

title: Stability Thresholds for Gravitationally Induced Entanglement in Shielded Setups
summary: Proposed experiments for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) typically suppress direct electromagnetic interactions between two massive particles by inserting a conducting Faraday shield. For superconducting particles, their large diamagnetism requires additional magnetic shielding to screen magnetic dipolar interactions. Here, we analyze the effect of residual particle-shield interactions and show that both Casimir and magnetic-dipole interactions can severely limit GIE tests by imprinting large phases. We quantify how run-to-run positional and orientational fluctuations of the setup elements, including the shield, trapping potentials, and detectors, convert these phases into effective decoherence, strongly reducing the detectable bipartite entanglement. In particular, we show that magnetic interactions between the particles and a superconducting shield constitute a major noise source, especially relevant for levitated superconducting particles. Treating the vibrational modes of the shield quantum mechanically, we further find that thermal vibrations generate persistent particle-shield correlations and can even mediate particle-particle entanglement that can mimic a gravitational signal. Finally, we derive quantitative thresholds on the maximum tolerable positional and orientational fluctuations of the setup elements required to observe entanglement, and propose mitigation strategies including geometry optimization and shield cooling to preserve a genuine GIE signature.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that residual Casimir and magnetic-dipole interactions between particles and shields in GIE experiments can severely limit detection of gravitationally induced entanglement, with thermal shield vibrations potentially mimicking gravitational signals; it provides quantitative stability thresholds and mitigation strategies.
AI.motivation: To analyze how residual particle-shield interactions (Casimir and magnetic-dipole) and setup fluctuations affect gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) experiments, particularly for superconducting particles where diamagnetism requires additional magnetic shielding.
AI.method: Quantitative analysis of Casimir and magnetic-dipole interactions between particles and shields; assessment of run-to-run positional/orientational fluctuations converting phases into decoherence; quantum mechanical treatment of shield vibrational modes; derivation of stability thresholds.
AI.result: Casimir and magnetic-dipole interactions imprint large phases that reduce detectable bipartite entanglement; magnetic interactions with superconducting shields are a major noise source; thermal shield vibrations generate persistent correlations and can mimic gravitational signals.
AI.conclusion: Quantitative thresholds on positional/orientational fluctuations are required for genuine GIE observation; proposed mitigation includes geometry optimization and shield cooling.

title: The Exact Replica Threshold for Nonlinear Moments of Quantum States
summary: Joint measurements on multiple copies of a quantum state provide access to nonlinear observables such as $\operatorname{tr}(ρ^t)$, but whether replica number marks a sharp information-theoretic resource boundary has remained unclear. For every fixed order $t\ge 3$, existing protocols show that $\lceil t/2\rceil$ replicas already suffice for polynomial-sample estimation of $\operatorname{tr}(ρ^t)$, yet it has remained open whether one fewer replica must necessarily incur a sample-complexity barrier growing with the dimension. We prove that this is indeed the case in the sample/copy-access model with replica-limited joint measurements: any protocol restricted to $\lceil t/2\rceil-1$ replicas requires dimension-growing sample complexity, while $\lceil t/2\rceil$ replicas suffice by prior work. Thus the exact replica threshold for fixed-order pure moments is $\lceil t/2\rceil$. Equivalently, for fixed-order pure moments, one additional coherent replica is not merely useful but marks the exact threshold between polynomial-sample estimation and a dimension-growing regime in the replica-limited model. We further show that the same threshold law extends to a broad family of observable-weighted moments $\operatorname{tr}(Oρ^t)$, including Pauli observables and other observables with bounded operator norm and macroscopic trace norm. Coherent replica number therefore acts as a genuinely discrete resource for nonlinear quantum-state estimation.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the exact replica threshold for estimating nonlinear functionals like $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^t)$ is $\lceil t/2\rceil$: using $\lceil t/2\rceil-1$ replicas requires dimension-growing sample complexity, while $\lceil t/2\rceil$ replicas suffice for polynomial-sample estimation. This threshold extends to observable-weighted moments $\operatorname{tr}(O\rho^t)$.
AI.motivation: To determine whether replica number constitutes a sharp information-theoretic resource boundary in nonlinear quantum state estimation, specifically whether the gap between $\lceil t/2\rceil-1$ and $\lceil t/2\rceil$ replicas marks a fundamental sample-complexity transition.
AI.method: The authors analyze the sample/copy-access model with replica-limited joint measurements, proving a lower bound showing that $\lceil t/2\rceil-1$ replicas force dimension-growing sample complexity, while leveraging prior work showing $\lceil t/2\rceil$ replicas suffice for polynomial-sample estimation. The results are extended to weighted moments $\operatorname{tr}(O\rho^t)$ for observables with bounded operator norm and macroscopic trace norm.
AI.result: The exact replica threshold for fixed-order pure moments is $\lceil t/2\rceil$. One additional coherent replica marks the boundary between polynomial-sample estimation and a dimension-growing regime. The same threshold extends to a broad family of observable-weighted moments.
AI.conclusion: Coherent replica number acts as a genuinely discrete resource for nonlinear quantum-state estimation, with a sharp threshold at $\lceil t/2\rceil$ replicas for estimating $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^t)$ and related observables.

title: Quantum Circuit Partitioning For Effective Utilization of Quantum Resources
summary: Near-term hardware is constrained by high error rates, small qubit counts, and relatively low output fidelity, making the execution of large, high performance quantum circuits difficult. Circuit partitioning (or circuit cutting) has emerged as a promising approach to circumvent these limitations by decomposing circuits into smaller subcircuits at two-qubit interaction points. However, it remains unclear which classes of circuits benefit the most from partitioning and under what hardware conditions it is most effective. In this work, we evaluate the suitability of quantum circuits for partitioning from three perspectives: improving fidelity, enabling distributed execution, and scaling to larger circuit sizes. Specifically, we compare uncut circuit execution against two circuit partitioning approaches: Qiskit's automatic cut finding technique and a custom performance optimized circuit cutting method. We also measure these across GHZ, QFT, brickwork, and random quantum circuits ranging from 4 to 14 qubits, using mean absolute error of expectation values and overall output fidelity. Our results show that partitioning benefits larger, highly interconnected circuits, with our custom method reducing error by up to 55\% and improve fidelity for GHZ circuits, but degrading performance for brickwork circuits at larger scales.

AI.tldr: This work evaluates circuit partitioning (cutting) for near-term quantum hardware, comparing Qiskit's automatic cut finding and a custom performance-optimized method across GHZ, QFT, brickwork, and random circuits (4–14 qubits). Results show partitioning benefits larger, highly interconnected circuits (e.g., GHZ error reduced by up to 55%), but can degrade performance for brickwork circuits at larger scales.
AI.motivation: Near-term quantum hardware suffers from high error rates, small qubit counts, and low fidelity, making large quantum circuit execution difficult. Circuit partitioning offers a way to circumvent these limitations, but it is unclear which circuit classes benefit most and under what hardware conditions partitioning is most effective.
AI.method: The authors compare uncut circuit execution against two partitioning approaches: Qiskit's automatic cut finding and a custom performance-optimized cutting method. They evaluate across GHZ, QFT, brickwork, and random quantum circuits (4–14 qubits) using mean absolute error of expectation values and overall output fidelity.
AI.result: Partitioning benefits larger, highly interconnected circuits. The custom method reduces error by up to 55% and improves fidelity for GHZ circuits, but degrades performance for brickwork circuits at larger scales.
AI.conclusion: Circuit partitioning is not universally beneficial; its effectiveness depends on circuit topology and scale. Highly interconnected circuits (e.g., GHZ) see significant gains, while certain structured circuits (e.g., brickwork) may suffer performance degradation.

title: Approaching the Limit of Quantum Clock Precision
summary: Precise and autonomous clocks are of fundamental interest and central importance to both foundational studies and practical applications. Here, we construct a blueprint for a quantum clock governed by time-independent interactions. By carefully-engineered coherent transport in dissipative spin chains, we achieve a scaling exponent at the precision-resolution trade-off fundamental bound, bringing this within reach of physically realistic and experimentally accessible systems. We further introduce a sudden-quench protocol that enables repeated operation through a simple initialization and detachment mechanism. Remarkably, the protocol is robust to imprecise detachment timing, implying that high-precision timekeeping can be achieved even when driven by a clock with much lower precision.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a blueprint for a quantum clock using time-independent interactions in dissipative spin chains, achieving the fundamental precision-resolution trade-off bound and introducing a robust sudden-quench protocol for repeated operation.
AI.motivation: Precise and autonomous clocks are of fundamental interest and central importance to both foundational studies and practical applications.
AI.method: Carefully-engineered coherent transport in dissipative spin chains achieves the scaling exponent at the precision-resolution trade-off fundamental bound. A sudden-quench protocol with simple initialization and detachment mechanism enables repeated operation.
AI.result: Achieved the fundamental precision-resolution trade-off bound scaling exponent within experimentally accessible systems. The sudden-quench protocol is robust to imprecise detachment timing.
AI.conclusion: High-precision timekeeping can be achieved even when driven by a clock with much lower precision, demonstrating robustness and practical feasibility.

title: Correlated Quantum Dephasometry: Symmetry-Resolved Noise Spectroscopy of Two-Dimensional Superconductors and Altermagnets
summary: Symmetry-resolved spectroscopies, such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and polarization-resolved Raman, are central for quantum material characterization, yet remain challenging at nanoscale dimensions and low frequencies. Here, we propose correlated quantum dephasometry, which enables symmetry resolved quantum noise spectroscopy of materials at nanoscale and low ($\sim$MHz) frequencies via correlated dephasing of two spin qubits near materials. Our approach leverages the finite-range spatial structures of nonlocal near-field noise correlations to isolate rotational symmetry of the material response in momentum space beyond single qubit capabilities. We apply our approach to two-dimensional (2D) superconductors, and predict clear fingerprints that discriminate s-, d-, and g-wave symmetry of the superconducting gap. To highlight the generality, we further show that the same framework resolves 2D s-wave antiferromagnets and d-wave altermagnets. Our results establish correlated quantum dephasometry as a nanoscale, low-frequency complement for symmetry-resolved spectroscopy applicable to a broad class of quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Correlated quantum dephasometry uses two spin qubits near materials to perform symmetry-resolved quantum noise spectroscopy at nanoscale and low (~MHz) frequencies, enabling discrimination of superconducting gap symmetries (s-, d-, g-wave) and magnetic orders (s-wave antiferromagnets, d-wave altermagnets).
AI.motivation: Symmetry-resolved spectroscopies like ARPES and Raman are central for quantum material characterization but remain challenging at nanoscale dimensions and low frequencies; this work aims to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: The approach uses correlated dephasing of two spin qubits near materials to probe nonlocal near-field noise correlations, leveraging their finite-range spatial structures to isolate rotational symmetry of material response in momentum space.
AI.result: Clear fingerprints discriminate s-, d-, and g-wave symmetry of superconducting gaps in 2D superconductors, and the framework resolves 2D s-wave antiferromagnets and d-wave altermagnets.
AI.conclusion: Correlated quantum dephasometry is established as a nanoscale, low-frequency complement for symmetry-resolved spectroscopy applicable to a broad class of quantum materials.
